planting.note: Set small container-grown plants in fall into rocky, well-drained foothill soil, or fall-sow fresh acorns directly where they are to grow since the developing taproot resents later disturbance.

directions: Mexican blue oak forms the open, parklike evergreen woodland of the foothills below the pine-oak belt in the Chiricahua, Huachuca, Santa Rita, and Santa Catalina Mountains, its small rounded leaves showing a distinct powdery blue-gray cast that sets it apart from the greener oaks sharing those slopes. It is among the most drought-tolerant oaks in cultivation, surviving on rocky, skeletal soils with only the rainfall a sky-island foothill naturally receives once its roots are a few years established. New leaves and twigs often flush with a soft pinkish or bronze tint before hardening to blue-green, giving it seasonal interest beyond its handsome winter silhouette. Give it full sun, sharp drainage, and room to develop a broad, low-branching crown, and avoid summer irrigation on an established tree, which does more harm than good.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Scarify or hot-water-soak seed before fall or spring sowing to break the hard coat, or set rooted cuttings into rocky, sharply drained canyon or foothill soil; growth is slow the first couple seasons while the root system establishes.

directions: Mearns' sumac is the large-leaved, glabrous Arizona form of evergreen sumac, found in rocky canyons and oak woodland of the Chiricahua, Huachuca, and Santa Rita Mountains, where its glossy, leathery, three-parted leaflets stay dark green year-round rather than dropping for winter. Dense upright clusters of small cream to pale yellow flowers open in late summer and ripen into fuzzy red berries that persist into winter and draw songbirds through the lean months. It tolerates rocky, lean soil and considerable drought once established, and can be grown as an informal screen, wildlife hedge, or background shrub in a dry foothill garden. Occasional thinning after fruiting keeps the naturally dense, rounded habit from becoming congested.

planting.note: Nick the hard seed coat and soak before sowing after the last frost in well-drained rocky soil; plants die back to a woody base after freezes further north in their range and resprout vigorously from the root crown in late spring.

directions: Western coral bean grows along rocky canyons and bajadas in the foothills of the Santa Rita, Pajarito, and Baboquivari Mountains, among the only places in the United States where this otherwise Mexican tree reaches north of the border. Showy upright spikes of waxy, deep red tubular flowers open on bare stems in late spring before the large three-parted leaves emerge, drawing hummingbirds from a distance, and the flowers are followed by dark pods holding a handful of poisonous bright red seeds. In the warmer parts of its range it can build into a small multi-trunked tree, but through most of southern Arizona's gardens hard freezes keep it a shrub that dies back to its woody base each winter and regrows strongly once warm weather returns. Grow it in full sun on lean, fast-draining soil and withhold water through its leafless winter dormancy.
